module.cookie_security.checks: Examines the cookies set by the home page and their Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite attributes.
module.cookie_security.fix:
Identify the flagged cookies (their names are in the finding) and what creates them: the application, its framework, the CMS, the load balancer or the CDN. The Application, Cookies tab of the browser developer tools (F12 key) shows the attributes of each one.
Add `Secure` to every cookie so that it is sent over HTTPS only. This assumes the whole site is on HTTPS (HTTP to HTTPS redirect, HSTS).
Add `HttpOnly` to session and authentication cookies so that the page's JavaScript cannot read them if a script is injected (XSS). Only a cookie that the site's JavaScript must read (for example a CSRF token read by a single-page application) can go without it, and it must never hold a session.
Add `SameSite=Lax` (or `Strict` for sensitive session cookies) to limit sending from other sites (CSRF). Use `SameSite=None` only if the cookie really has to be sent in a third-party context (iframe, cross-domain single sign-on): it then requires `Secure`.
Set these attributes at the source, in the application or framework configuration (see the snippet for PHP, Express, Django and ASP.NET Core). For a cookie set by a product you do not control, look for its "secure / httponly" setting in its administration.
If the application cannot be changed, add the attributes at the reverse proxy (nginx and Apache snippets). They then apply to every cookie, including those the site's JavaScript must read: check that nothing breaks.
For the session cookie, prefer the `__Host-` prefix (for example `__Host-session`): the browser then accepts it only with `Secure`, without a `Domain` attribute and with `Path=/`.
Check: `curl -sI https://example.com | grep -i set-cookie` must show `Secure`, `HttpOnly` and `SameSite` on every cookie; sign in to also check the session cookie set after authentication, then run the scan again.
module.cookie_security.title: Cookies
module.cookie_security.why: A session cookie without these attributes can be stolen by an injected script, intercepted over HTTP or replayed from another site (CSRF).
